core: Abstraction as a range of visual strategies that simplify, reorganize, distort, or remove recognizable references
The distinction between near-abstraction and non-representational or non-objective work
Line, color, shape, scale, material, title, and display as evidence for analysis
supporting: Early twentieth-century modernist claims about abstract art
The limits of asking who made the first abstract artwork
Non-representational visual traditions before and beyond Euro-American modernism
outOfScope: A complete chronology of modernism or catalogue of abstract movements
A claim that abstraction has no content, feeling, politics, context, or historical reference
A claim that non-representational art is automatically universal or culturally neutral
Treating a title as the only evidence for a work's source or meaning

claims.claim: Abstraction exists on a spectrum: a work can pull away from natural appearances while retaining an identifiable source, or it can be non-representational and begin without reference to natural objects.

The question of who made the first abstract artwork is difficult to resolve because works can be progressively abstracted, titles and documentation affect interpretation, and the question often narrows a longer global history.
Modern artists including Mondrian and van Doesburg developed work through gradual abstraction from recognizable sources as well as through non-representational composition.

Non-representational visual traditions have a longer and broader history than a narrow modern-European firstness story, including Islamic manuscript and decorative traditions discussed by Smarthistory.
An abstract work can organize attention through relations among color, line, shape, texture, rhythm, scale, material, and space even when it does not depict a recognizable subject.

A responsible interpretation starts with what is visible and documented, then uses titles, preparatory studies, artist statements, exhibition context, and historical evidence to make limited claims about reference or meaning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Abstract art is frequently described either as art with no subject or as a uniquely modern European invention.
positions: Some works are non-representational, and twentieth-century artists made explicit claims for new forms of abstraction.
Other works retain transformed sources, and non-representational visual traditions predate and exceed the narrow modernist story.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson distinguishes degrees of abstraction from pure non-representation, treats firstness as a limited historical question, and asks for object-specific evidence before assigning a source or meaning.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft defined abstract art as a generic course concept and offered no distinction between degrees of abstraction, no historical context, and no evidence-based assessment.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with an original, source-grounded explanation of abstraction as a spectrum.
Added the difference between near-abstraction and non-representational art.
Corrected the narrow first-abstract-artwork narrative by naming its evidence and global-history limits.
Added a procedure for interpreting formal relationships without inventing a hidden subject and supplied five four-option questions.
rightsIssues: The two Smarthistory sources are used as REFERENCE_ONLY. No source prose or images are reproduced; all lesson text and questions are original synthesis.
